extractor.note: Partial pass over §§ 8, 12, 17 of the main text and Sections 1 and 3 of the Nachwort.

coverage_note: Covers §§ 8, 12 and 17 (rational psychology and phenomenology, and the significance of ontological concepts for psychology) together with Sections 1 and 3 of the Nachwort. The remaining sections carrying hits are not covered.

units.claim: An eidetic reduction can be performed that excludes all questions of real existence and turns research to the eidos, for instance the essence perception.
units.quote: we can also perform an “eidetic reduction” — exclude all questions of real existence and carry out purely eidetic research

units.claim: Whoever cannot carry out the phenomenological reductions and grasp pure consciousness as idea is barred from entry into transcendental phenomenology and into philosophy in general.
units.quote: who cannot carry out the phenomenological reductions and grasp the pure, absolutely posited experience, the pure consciousness as idea — for him, entry into transcendental phenomenology and into philosophy in general is barred

units.claim: Only through reduction to pure consciousness is the absolute to be won, the absolute relatum for all realities, whose being is throughout relative.
units.quote: only through reduction to this is the “absolute” to be won, the absolute relatum for all realities, whose being is throughout relative being

units.claim: Every description of psychic experiences passes into a purely phenomenological one through an ideally possible reduction that is both eidetic and purifying from realization.
units.quote: every description of psychic experiences passes, through the ideally possible reduction (eidetic and purifying from realization), into a purely phenomenological one

units.claim: Transcendental experience becomes possible only through a radical change of the attitude in which natural worldly experience runs its course, a change called phenomenological reduction.
units.quote: Transcendental experience becomes possible only through a radical change of the attitude in which natural, worldly experience runs its course — a change called “phenomenological reduction.”

units.claim: The attitude-change called the reduction is performed by the philosophizing person from the natural attitude in which one experiences oneself as a human person living among others in the world.
units.quote: The attitude-change called phenomenological reduction is performed by the philosophizing person from the natural attitude in which one experiences oneself as a human person living among others in the world.
